We completed the QRH with the help of both the FO and Captain to reach some switches and work through nuances of the situation. I assisted the FO with some of the ACARS messages and general airfield study. While we were accomplishing these tasks, the Captain quickly descended out of FL340 and got established on ILS final for Runway XX. We executed an uneventful flaps 50 landing about 14 minutes after receiving the initial cargo fire indications. We then taxied to the south ramp where we were inspected by the emergency services on the taxi in. The cause of this priority was multiple level 3 alerts. Maintenance said the MSC failed causing false level 3 alerts.
ASRSN:1951477.s: The RFO, Captain, and First Officer of Aircraft X executed an emergency descent from FL340 and landed after receiving false Level 3 cargo fire and smoke alerts. Maintenance determined the alerts were caused by a failed MSC, resulting in an uneventful landing and subsequent inspection.

ASRSN:1951502.n: Upon departure as the Pilot Flying, we were climbing through 3,500 feet, and the Master Caution Illuminated. Upon request of the Captain, we initiated a transfer of flight controls, and I contacted ATC to inform them we needed to turn back to the airport. It was determined that the Master Caution was associated with the Main Cargo Door Unlocked Light, which was illuminated. ATC instructed us to level out at 6,000 feet, at which point we requested to level out at 4,000 ft to Expedite our return to the airport. ATC then directed us to continue our decent down to 2,500 feet. At some point in this portion of the descent, the cargo door unlock light went out. We performed an ILS, and landing on Runway XX with no further issue. Final cross check with Loaders that he announced that cabin reports which was all locks up and cabin secured, then Captain said parking brake set per SOM, then push back as scheduled on time, as Captain we checked all lights and EICAS massages and checklist before taxi. Upon departure as the pilot monitoring, We were climbing through 3,500 feet and the Master Caution Illuminated. Upon request of the Captain, we initiated a transfer of flight controls and contacted ATC to inform them we needed to turn back to the airport. It was determined that the Master Caution was associated with the Main Cargo Door Unlocked Light, which was illuminated. ATC instructed us to level out at 6,000 feet, at which point we requested to level out at 4,000 feet to expedite our return to the airport. ATC then directed us to continue our decent down to 2,500 feet. At some point in this portion of the descent, the Cargo Door Unlocked Light went out. We performed a ILS approach, and landing on runway XX with no further issue.
ASRSN:1951502.s: During climb through 3,500 feet, the crew returned to the airport after the Main Cargo Door Unlocked light illuminated. The light extinguished during descent to 2,500 feet, and the aircraft landed safely on Runway XX with no further issues.

ASRSN:1951576.n: After descending through 10,000 ft. the Flight Attendant was walking through the aisle to prepare the cabin for landing and smelled a dirty sock/musty fume in the mid to forward cabin. The fume lasted for approximately 10 minutes. The smell was observed by both Flight Attendants up front. The fume was not smelled in the flight deck. The Captain was notified of the smell after landing due to the proximity to landing when the smell was observed. This was the second write-up for fumes in the cabin within approximately 1 week of our event. After a fume write-up, the maintenance procedure should include measuring the air quality in the flight deck and cabin with a device that can objectively determine if organophospates and carbon monoxide is still present. Each person's olfactory is different and subjective, and relying on one or two maintenance techs' sense of smell determine if the fume is still present is not an objective, safe, or accurate procedure to clear the airplane back to fly.
ASRSN:1951576.s: Flight attendants detected a musty fume in the cabin during descent below 10,000 ft, which lasted 10 minutes and was not smelled in the flight deck. The reporter recommends using objective air quality testing for organophosphates and carbon monoxide instead of relying on subjective maintenance smell checks.

ASRSN:1951587.n: On descent into the approach pattern to ZZZZ, received ECIAS Messages: Flaps Primary Fail and Slats Drive. Captain was Pilot Flying and First Officer completed all electronic checklists, referenced advisory landing distance and then completed normal landing checklist. Pilot Flying was vectoring around buildups and receiving vectors, and changing runways in FMS. Lowering gear checklist item was accomplished around 1,100 feet. Received gear warning. Acknowledged and continued since gear was in transit. Gear confirmed down and locked at 700 feet. Taken further vectors off approach until landing checklist was completed. Captain was Pilot Flying. On arrival into ZZZZ. Vectoring for spacing, slowing, and CBs. During initial configuration, simultaneously received EICAS messages: FLAPS PRIMARY FAIL and SLATS DRIVE. Completed all electronic checklists, and referenced advisory landing distance. During checklists, received a runway change and approach clearance. In VMC. Gear down was not accomplished before 1,000 AFL. Configured and stable by 500 AFL. Uneventful landing. Possibly a Slat sensor that was on a MEL placard for nine days? Slat sensor MEL placard could have been fixed and cleared?
ASRSN:1951587.s: The Captain flew a descent into ZZZZ where simultaneous Flaps Primary Fail and Slats Drive EICAS messages occurred. The crew completed checklists, delayed gear extension until 1,100 feet, and executed an uneventful landing, suspecting a potentially cleared Slat sensor MEL issue.

ASRSN:1951607.n: After takeoff upon raising gear we encountered L MAIN gear UNSAFE(RED) and secondary UNSAFE (Red) indication on configuration page. We slowed to 190 knots and leveled at 5,000 feet. Requested vectors to remain in local area in event of turn back. First Officer flew and assumed radio duties while Captain consulted QRH and contacted Dispatch and Maintenance. Captain ran the QRH - GEAR PRIMARY OR SECONDARY LIGHTS ILLUMINATED WITH GEAR HANDLE UP. Proceeded with QRH and was able to work problem to flyable condition. Obtained new fuel burn numbers and determined that continuing to ZZZ was best option. After gear up, Captain (Pilot Monitoring) noticed left main landing gear light flickering on and off. Checked configuration page to confirm finding. Gear was also flickering on and off on configuration page. Informed [approach] we needed to stay low and slow as we ran QRH and coordinated with Company. Requested vectors and altitude for safety and eventual return to ZZZ1. Captain coordinated with Company Dispatcher and Maintenance. I flew the airplane and handled radios. After running the QRH and a couple of recommendations from maintenance, it was determined it was safe to continue to ZZZ. We then coordinated with ATC to resume on course.
ASRSN:1951607.s: The crew encountered left main gear unsafe indications after takeoff while leveling at 5,000 feet. After consulting the QRH and maintenance, they resolved the issue and safely continued to ZZZ.

ASRSN:1951611.n: Report submitted due to no cell connectivity at divert location. Coasting out over Ocean on HF at FL340 fire bells and alerts with messages stating CABIN SMOKE, CRG FIRE LWR AFT, CRG FIRE LWR FWD and all upper cargo smoke detectors indicating smoke. Turned right to head to cold bay while Captain got [Relief Officer] back to cockpit and instructed Load master to don his oxygen mask. Captain took over flying duties and delegated QRH to [Relief Officer], and to me he delegated radios and setting up approach into new destination, and communication with [Dispatcher] on ACARS. Captain performed an emergency descent and approach while the [relief officer] and I worked the QRH and I got clearance and set up approach. FSS had emergency equipment standing by the time we arrived. I believe we were on the ground within 12-14 minutes. After the event we think electrical controller gave false fire and smoke indications - during the event we thought there was a fire in lower cargo where the only cargo was on the aircraft.
ASRSN:1951611.s: The crew experienced false cargo fire and smoke alerts at FL340 over the ocean, likely caused by an electrical controller malfunction. They executed an emergency descent and diverted to a cold bay, landing within 12–14 minutes with emergency equipment standing by.

ASRSN:1951684.n: I was the B-FA (Flight Attendant) and while setting up my galley cart the FWD Lav smoke alarm went off. Captain called FAs to confirm FWD Lav smoke alarm indicators are going off. A few moments after Captain called I saw a passenger walk out of the Lav and I saw A FA confront the woman as she walked out of the Lav and the FWD smoke alarm deactivated. I went up to FWD lav when I saw the passenger sit down. It smelled like hard chemicals or like a burning rubber smell. The smell gave me a headache of smelling it as well my eyes started watering after staying there for longer than a few minutes. Captain called up to confirm since the alarm deactivated there was no need to divert and to continue to ZZZ1 where authorities would be meeting us at the gate. Once landed passenger was escorted by authorities off the airplane.
ASRSN:1951684.s: A flight attendant reported a forward lavatory smoke alarm activation caused by a passenger, which deactivated after the passenger exited. The crew continued to ZZZ1 without diverting, where authorities met the aircraft to escort the passenger off following a chemical smell and eye irritation.

ASRSN:1951695.n: Prepared a Defibrillator for shipment from ZZZ to ZZZ1 by Person A on Date, followed Hazmat Raps instruction for packaging and labeling. shipped Company 2 day express.Not knowing Company is an air method of shipping and believing it is ground shipping method.More training and coaching to improve on Hazmat raps and the different methods of Company shipping.
ASRSN:1951695.s: Person A prepared a defibrillator for shipment from ZZZ to ZZZ1, following Hazmat Raps instructions but mistakenly believing the carrier used ground transport instead of air. The reporter identified a need for additional training on Hazmat regulations and carrier shipping methods to prevent future errors.

ASRSN:1951701.n: On Day 0 at XC50, Aircraft X went AOG at APA for WOW MISCOMPARE Amber CAS: 'After Takeoff landing gear would not retract. After several attempts to retract gear WOW MISCOMPARE Amber CAS message was generated'. At XD32, I requested the aircraft to be placed into hanger to thaw. I informed Maintenance Control that we would not be able to do gear swings with absence of a hydraulic mule. At XD39, Person A in Maintenance Control responded that we could do with the aux pump if needed and attached Cessna letter XXXXXXXX. At XJ16, I sent a message informing Maintenance Control that the aircraft finally made it into the hanger and that we still need a Maintenance Manual (MM) reference for performing the gear swings with the aux pump. At XJ29, Person C at Maintenance Control replied that he would look into finding a reference, and if he could not find one that he would inquire Person B for support documentation. At XK35, Person D sent an email expressing his concern for an approved procedure that allows us to deviate from what is written in the MM. At XK53, Person C sent an email stating that they were not looking to have all the operational gear swing checks complied with but just wanted to make sure the gear will go up and locked and come back down and locked. He added that if we weren't comfortable with doing this that they could pursue a special ferry permit. At XK57, Person D replied, please pursue working on a Special Ferry Permit. At XL32, Person C responded that they were going to look for another vendor and would not prefer to ferry due to an improper preflight. At XM03, Maintenance Control notified us that they were going to seek a vendor as an assist for a hydraulic mule and don't close out our paperwork. On Day 1, XA49, we received an email from Person E stating that after speaking with Person F and Maintenance Control, that they felt that the letter from Cessna was acceptable for use to continue the directed maintenance. At XA50, Person E called us to follow up on his email and stated to get the aircraft back to the customer. At XB16, Person D and I spoke with Person F and he in turn sent us an email granting his authority to use the aircraft aux pump to perform a gear swing to assure proper gear indications. We went ahead and complied with the maintenance as directed.Maintenance Control directed us to perform gear swings per a correspondence letter XXXXXXXX dated 2 years ago from Cessna that references servicing of the hydraulic system per chapter 29. No where in the letter does it explicitly state that the aux pump can be used to swing the gear. There is no maintenance manual reference that states that you can use the aux pump to swing the gear. On Day 1 at XD17, spoke with Person G with Cessna and he informed Person D and I that gear swings with the aux pump is not prohibited but is not recommended. Person D and I did not feel comfortable with deviating from the maintenance manual and felt that the letter from Cessna lacked intent and was ambiguous. If any form of gear swing is prohibited with the hydraulic aux pump, the MM should state this or a more explicit letter from Cessna should be prepared. We were placed under utmost human factors of stress and duress from Maintenance Controls and our Supervisors to go against years of safety training and to speak up when put into a compromising position. Only after our phone call with Person F did we feel that we could execute the maintenance requested with his authority.
ASRSN:1951701.s: Pilots and Maintenance Control faced an AOG due to a WOW MISCOMPARE after takeoff at XC50. Under pressure, the crew performed gear swings using the auxiliary pump based on a Cessna letter, despite lacking explicit Maintenance Manual approval and concerns about safety compliance.

ASRSN:1951703.n: This airport is subject to strong Santa Ana winds from the north at certain times of the year, for which Runway 16/34 was built. Most GA aircraft can handle this configuration in a strong wind. However, there are buildings and vegetation obscuring the south 1400 feet of this runway from Tower view. Decades ago, the FAA installed a remote camera with a view down the runway with a monitor in the Tower cab to assist in preventing vehicle or pedestrian incursions. We are not allowed to use the camera as an aircraft separation device per the FAA, and it is written into our SOP's. Last October (2021), the camera failed. Since then, for over a year, the FAA has refused to repair the device as they cannot find any rule that permits its use. After multiple inquiries from Tower personnel asking when we would have a camera to resume safe operations on Runway 16/34, the FAA produced a letter prohibiting the use of Runway 16/34 for fixed wing aircraft UFN (until further notice). As far as we know, nothing has been done and we have no feedback. We are now in the Santa Ana season, and have had several cumulative days of north winds. We cannot designate 16/34 as the active runway despite the wind favoring its use. Aircraft must land on the cross Runway 9/27, in very strong crosswinds. The local pilots are asking why we cannot clear them to land on the safer runway, and we have no answer. Some of the landings/takeoffs I have seen with these strong crosswinds have been scary, to say the least. We have six flight schools at this airport, with pilots of little experience. It is a matter of time before an accident occurs. The FAA must immediately resolve this unsafe situation largely caused by their own hand.
ASRSN:1951703.s: Air traffic controllers reported that FAA refusal to repair a failed remote camera led to a prohibition on using Runway 16/34 during strong Santa Ana winds. Consequently, inexperienced pilots from six flight schools are forced to land on crosswind Runway 9/27, creating an unsafe situation the controller fears will cause an accident.

ASRSN:1951704.n: 1. L ENGINE CHIP white Crew Alert System at FL340 in VMC After confirming no action was required by QRH (white advisory message), continued climb to FL430. 2. Loud boom and aircraft yawing and light shaking at FL430 IN VMC (approximately 145 miles outside of departure point ZZZ and 85 miles to ZZZ1) 3. Reduced power on both engines and depressed control wheel master to maintain direction control. ATC was informed of the situation. Both crew members cross checked and confirmed it was the left engine was the issue. 4. Upon reducing the left engine to idle, Aural Warning 'Left Engine Fire' and accompanied by light smoke in cockpit. Oxygen mask were donned by both crew members with 100% oxygen selected and crew communication was established. 5. Memory items completed and left engine was secured. 6. No more left engine fire indication and smoke dissipated After confirming visually that smoke was not visible crew members removed oxygen mask one at a time. 7. Continued with emergency checklist and descent in VMC8. Entered IMC at around 5,000 feet, temperature well above freezing (above 10 degrees centigrade), and proceeded with single engine ILS into ZZZ1. 9. Single engine landing at ZZZ1 on Runway XXR and taxi to signature under own power.
ASRSN:1951704.s: The flight crew experienced a left engine fire and smoke at FL430, triggering an emergency descent and single-engine landing at ZZZ1. After securing the engine and completing memory items, they executed a safe ILS approach and taxi under own power.

ASRSN:1951723.n: My student (private pilot) and I were descending from our prescribed FOM procedures for a landing back for Runway XX at ZZZ. Our procedures state that we must execute a right descending turn from 2500 ft. MSL to 2000 ft. MSL (originally heading 180 degrees to a 45 degree entry to enter the traffic pattern for Runway XX). As we were on the 45 degree entry descending down to 2000 ft. MSL, I (the instructor) was worried about traffic that was departing the pattern. Not only was the traffic a concern, it was also night (visually seeing the traffic was a little challenging). As my student was flying the plane and I was looking to see what the traffic was planning to do, I also had my eyes set for the runway. I kept glancing at my student's altitude and I noticed we were still descending (past from 2000 ft. MSL). I verbally said 'watch your altitude' to my student in hopes that we would maintain 2000 ft. MSL, however, this was not the case. We continued a descent and I kept verbalizing to 'watch your altitude.' (I was still scanning for traffic and determining our relative position). It was not until we were at 1637 ft. MSL until I took the yoke to initiate the climb again. After the climb, we entered the traffic pattern safely and landed back to ZZZ without injury. As we were taxing back to the ramp, I was concerned about the event and had FAR 91.119 (Minimum Safe Altitudes) in the back of my mind. Later that night, I filed a safety report through our school's safety reporting system and requested that my student also send one in. Our safety manager at the school provided both of us (instructor and student) data on the flight itself. Our lowest altitude that we descended down to was 1637.1 ft. MSL while the descent lasted for 23 seconds. Though the descent was not acceptable per our school procedures nor by the FARs, I brought up the 'black hole illusion' to my student and included it in the original safety report. I brought this up because I believe that this illusion had a factor in the delay in altitude recovery. Because our 45 degree to downwind for Runway XX is primarily over all trees, it was all dark where we had no close sense to what our altitude was just by looking outside the aircraft. This was because it was very dark outside. The data also showed that our FPM was originally ~800 fpm which eventually increased to ~1250 fpm. This was speculated from the safety report that he might have pushed the yoke forward to scan for traffic after leaning forward (which the student stated they did). I do feel that the 'black hole illusion' was a major factor, but with the addition to radio calls, traffic scanning, night VFR flying, and position finding all contributed to the descent. Concern was for violating 91.119 (Minimum Safe Altitudes). Our safety manager stated that the trees we were over were estimated to be at ~488 ft. meaning we were only ~438 ft. above the tree tops which is lower than the 500 ft. minimum. Our safety manager briefed myself on the report and I briefed my student on the situation and why it is also important to not only look out for traffic, but also be scanning your instruments. I briefed my student on 91.119 and how it pertains to us and my student and I looked at our flight path and saw how low we ended up going. I required my student to also file a report as well. In conclusion, night VFR flying needs to be treated heavier on emphasis in regards to scanning your instruments. Night flying will add additional errors / illusions that maybe the instructor might not be entirely familiar with, but also for the student. There is also no excuse for an instructor (like myself) to oversee how low we both got. This was a learning experience for both myself and my student and heavier situational awareness will have to be acquired for future flights. My instructor and I were coming back on the XX corridor, passing the grain elevator and descending after passing the highway. During the descending S turn over the red barn there was departing traffic. While descending to 2,000 ft., I was looking at the traffic, leaned forward to see where they were at and continued my descent past 2,000. When I realized the traffic was not a factor I was at 1637.1 ft. This a problem due to we were already at a low altitude being in the corridor and I descending way below 2,000 ft. This is very important to never do again because of the main safety issue being altitude. It was also dark out and it is even more important to be aware of my current surroundings. A way to correct and fix this to make sure this does not happen ever again is to properly scan my instruments, especially my altimeter to make sure I do not descend past 2,000 ft. It was dark out and with night illusions being a very serious issue, we were over a dark area.With a dark area with not many lights, there is a night illusion called the black hole illusion. That is what is especially important to keep an eye on your altimeter to make sure you do not get disoriented when flying.
ASRSN:1951723.s: An instructor and student pilot descended below the required 2,000 ft MSL to 1,637 ft MSL during a night approach due to traffic scanning, leaning forward, and black hole illusion. The event resulted in a violation of FAR 91.119 minimum safe altitudes, though the aircraft landed safely after the instructor took control.

ASRSN:1951781.n: Descending into ZZZ for practice IAPs on IFR flight plan under VMC, I was cleared via radar vectors on final approach course for the VOR Runway XX. ZZZ Approach cleared me the approach and had me switch to Tower, shortly after checking in with Tower, the VPSS glide path on the G1000 had me initiate a descent out of 2000 ft. to the FAF altitude of 1400 ft. The descent angle put ZZZ1 Runway XX directly in front of me at a steep angle, which I mistook for ZZZ Runway XX. I inadvertently descended thru 1400 ft. and received a low altitude alert from ZZZ Tower. I acknowledged the alert with 'correcting, thank you;' arrested the descent at 1000 ft. within a mile of ZZZ1 with no pattern traffic noted, and climbed back to 1400 ft. The remainder of the IAP and sortie was uneventful.I was flying in primary reference to the approach plate, which does not depict ZZZ1 inside the IAF even though that airport has an identical runway alignment with ZZZ.
ASRSN:1951781.s: A pilot descending for a VOR approach at ZZZ mistakenly identified the nearby ZZZ1 runway due to similar alignment and descended below the 1400 ft FAF altitude. After receiving a low altitude alert from Tower, the pilot arrested the descent at 1000 ft and climbed back to 1400 ft, attributing the error to the approach plate not depicting ZZZ1.

ASRSN:1951782.n: During initial climbout, landing gear handle did not come up. Got stuck in the down position. Returned to the airport.
ASRSN:1951782.s: During initial climbout, the landing gear handle failed to retract and remained stuck in the down position. The pilot returned to the airport.

ASRSN:1951784.n: During preflight and taxi, everything was working normally. Nothing was out of the ordinary. I taxied from the FBO to Runway XX via Alpha. I proceeded to execute my engine run up. Again, nothing seemed to be wrong. After about 4 takeoffs and 2 landings ahead of me, I began to start the takeoff. I pushed full throttle but the plane seemed to be slow in accelerating. There was engine roughness and aggressive shaking. It has happened before where there has been some slowness in acceleration and engine roughness but as soon as you get off the ground, everything is good. I also thought it could be the nose wheel shaking, causing the shaking of the plane. I reached 50 KIAS and rotated. As I rotated, the stall horn squeaked. I lowered the nose and attempted to gain airspeed to climb. However, the rate of climb was extremely slow. I noticed the RPMs have not increased past 2,100 RPM. With this as well as severe engine roughness, I decided I needed to return to the airport.I made the radio call as follows: 'Tower, Aircraft X is facing extreme engine roughness and is struggling to climb. We would like to return to Runway XX'. The controller advised me to turn downwind when able. The height to turn downwind is 700 feet and the elevation of the land under the downwind leg is around 500 feet. I was unable to climb higher than 400 feet in the two minutes I had been in the air. I then said, Aircraft X, we are not able to climb high enough um is it possible for me to turn around and land on Runway XY?, which is the opposing runway of XX. The controller approved this and cleared me to land on Runway XY. I turned around while configuring for landing. He asked if I needed any assistance to which I said that I did not. I never requested priority handling because the engine was still running just not at full power. I landed safely and taxied back to the FBO via Alpha. I shut down the engine and downed the aircraft to get maintenance to look at it.
ASRSN:1951784.s: The pilot experienced severe engine roughness and limited acceleration during takeoff, with RPMs failing to exceed 2,100 and climb capped at 400 feet. After requesting and receiving clearance to land on the opposing runway, the pilot executed a safe landing and returned to the FBO for maintenance inspection.

ASRSN:1951793.n: After flying to the airport and making a full stop landing I taxied back for a routine takeoff. During climb out the engine began to run rough and had a significant power loss. Based on my altitude and distance from the departure airport I turned and reentered the traffic pattern. I completed the emergency/engine failure checklist and switched fuel tanks. A [request for priority handling] on the CTAF as I was in the traffic pattern. Position reports in the traffic pattern were made on the CTAF. A normal landing was made. At the FBO/maintenance facility a cylinder compression check was done with low compression noted. It was later determined that a valve failed.
ASRSN:1951793.s: The pilot experienced significant power loss and rough running during climbout due to a failed engine valve. After switching fuel tanks and requesting priority handling on CTAF, the pilot reentered the traffic pattern and completed a normal landing.

ASRSN:1951796.n: The C172 in question and I had each other in sight and were communicating. We were on right base with apparent equal distance to final. Upon extending my landing gear I had an anti-skid system failure alert. Not an emergency - however, asked the other plane for priority to land with this problem. The other pilot said 'no' to my priority request and stated, 'You just think you should have priority because you are faster;' or words to that effect. I then stated that I need to land immediately. I asked him to go around several times… another aircraft obliged and made a 360, but not the aircraft in question. We made our turn to final while still communicating back and forth… I had him in sight and continued. The other aircraft flew over top of us but we both had each other in sight and were in constant communication. Due to being a dark night, I saw the lights of the other aircraft but was not able to judge the distance. I continually stressed that I needed to land immediately and was going to get to the airport first. Both aircraft maintained visual and radio communications throughout. The other pilot was belligerent and uncooperative throughout. I was flying an Eclipse jet with passenger witnesses.
ASRSN:1951796.s: An Eclipse jet pilot with an anti-skid failure requested landing priority from a C172 on right base at night, but the C172 pilot refused and remained belligerent. Both aircraft maintained visual and radio contact while the Eclipse landed first, though the C172 flew over the Eclipse during the approach.

ASRSN:1951801.n: Using Foreflight I identified the Tower and UNICOM frequencies, and believed since Tower was inoperative during my flight, the UNICOM frequency XXX.XX was what I should be relaying my pattern positions on. The aircraft ADSB In was inop and I was using a STRATUX linked to my IPAD for traffic awareness. I was operating with landing lights, nav lights, and strobe lights on. After not hearing radio communications on UNICOM , I switched to Tower while I was approaching the pattern and made a call in the blind to Tower, XXX.XY. I received no reply and after listening for a bit, heard no other communications so switched back to UNICOM , XXX.XX. I saw an aircraft on my iPad--stratux, looked like on final. However, I had been reporting my pattern position and had heard no one else reporting. I could not pick other aircraft up visually, but it looked like it might have been on a straight-in final. I turned left base, still not seeing the other aircraft, so I rolled out a bit and flattened my descent to stay above until I could pick up visually. During the rollout, I saw the other aircraft (believe a Cherokee), in a steep avoidance turn to my left and below. I was not sure it was an avoidance turn, so I started a climbing right hand turn to get above pattern altitude and get east of the field. I returned to pattern after noting the aircraft had landed. After landing the FBO operator came out and mentioned that I should have been on Tower frequency and that had seen a light on their receiver indicating someone was communicating on UNICOM . I understand now that C on a VFR sectional next to a frequency means that is the common traffic advisory frequency to use.
ASRSN:1951801.s: A VFR pilot operating with inoperative ADSB In and using a Stratux for traffic awareness misidentified the CTAF frequency while approaching the pattern. This led to a near mid-air collision with a Cherokee on final, prompting the pilot to climb and exit the pattern before the other aircraft landed.

ASRSN:1951806.n: I was VFR enroute from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. After departing ZZZ1 I contacted ZZZ Approach for traffic advisory on any commercial traffic enroute to ZZZ. I was assigned a discrete transponder code and handed off to ZZZ2 Tower for a midfield crossing south-north over ZZZ2. After crossing ZZZ2 midfield, ZZZ2 Tower advised me to contact ZZZ advisory frequency. I made my first call on the advisory frequency and indicated I was 1 NM east of ZZZ and entering left downwind for Runway X. After passing Runway X threshold on downwind another aircraft announced they were 'setting up for a left base'. I made visual contact with the aircraft, which was on an extended left base for Runway X (approximately 2 miles west of the threshold of Runway X). I announced I would extend my downwind for spacing for the aircraft on left base.I announced and turned left base after the previous aircraft was ~1/4 NM from the threshold of Runway X. I then announced 3 NM final for Runway X. Within a few seconds of that call, I heard another aircraft announce left base for Runway X. As I was descending on final I visually identified another aircraft turning final for Runway X off my port side at my altitude and a few plane lengths ahead. I called out to the aircraft turning final and advised I was already on final and suggested they break off their approach. There was no reply from the other aircraft. The other aircraft continued approaching my port side and when they were within ~100 ft. laterally I announced a balked landing. I was crossing over the freeway at approximately 200 ft. MSL at the time. I applied power, made a climbing 180-degree right turn over the river and climbed to approximately 400 ft. MSL while attempting to stay within the SFRA and outside the Class C airspace over the river. I listened and visually verified no traffic in the pattern on left base for Runway X announced a right base for Runway X and landed without further incident. While this was my first time landing at ZZZ I had briefed FAR Part 93 for air traffic rules and communications within the SFRA prior to departing ZZZ1 and was in contact with ZZZ ATC en route. After searching FlightAware it appears as if the other aircraft was performing a low approach or touch and go at ZZZ just after I had entered left downwind for Runway X. I do not know if they heard my call for extended downwind for Runway X but my best guess is that they did not, as they turned base while I was on extended final and turned final into my flight path.
ASRSN:1951806.s: A VFR pilot executing a landing at ZZZ airport encountered a conflicting aircraft on final approach that ignored radio calls to break off. The pilot performed a balked landing at 200 ft MSL due to the other aircraft turning final into their flight path, likely because the second pilot did not hear the spacing announcement.

ASRSN:1951845.n: While flying aircraft and landing at ZZZ on our last flight of the day on Runway XX, crosswinds were 200 degrees and 11 kts. Upon touchdown in touchdown zone, I was slightly left of center line on rollout. Aircraft drifted right off center line during application of reverse. Captain assumed control of aircraft. Taxi and shutdown were uneventful.
ASRSN:1951845.s: The pilot reported that while landing an aircraft on Runway XX at ZZZ in 11-knot crosswinds, the aircraft drifted right of the centerline during reverse thrust application. The Captain assumed control, and the subsequent taxi and shutdown were uneventful.

ASRSN:1951887.n: Landed 34R in SLC uneventfully with planned taxi off at H8. We had briefed a taxi plan of F to B to 2W for the ramp. We were given by Tower a 'H7 approved, H to H6 to 2V East;' taxi clearance. Based on the airport pages and the 10-9 page it looks as though you still cannot enter the ramp from the east. I made the turn south onto H7 to H then switched over to the AMM display and saw there was a 2 East entry to the ramp. I was still confused by the H to H6 clearance and decided just to make the turn towards 2East. We switched to ramp and received clearance to our gate. I just wanted to bring the 10-9 issue up because it clearly needs to be updated, and I'm wondering why Tower issued the H6 clearance when it looks as though H6 ends at H.
ASRSN:1951887.s: The pilot landed at SLC and received a taxi clearance via H6 that conflicted with airport diagrams showing H6 ends at H. The crew bypassed the confusing clearance to enter the ramp via 2 East, noting the 10-9 page requires updating.

ASRSN:1951894.n: We were pushing off [Gate] X in BNA and called on the 'Ramp' frequency per procedures, because this is where we should have critical flight procedures, no answer (as usual) since there is not an actual Ramp Controller. No one answered, we pushed, another aircraft was trying to taxi into [Gate] Y, our tug stopped, unsure of where the other aircraft was headed, finally we figured out what was going on, we were waiting for him and he was waiting for us. We ended up pushing very deep to give him room. It all worked out fine but BNA still needs a Ramp Controller. I sent in at least one other report, maybe two, over the past couple of years. This situation with the BNA ramp is unsatisfactory and will cause bent metal (I think it already has, maybe more than once). How many multi-million dollar wing-to-wing or winglet-to-tail or airplane-to airplane collisions are we going to accept before we realize that it's cheaper and SAFER to hire a Ramp Controller. The airport needs to do it, and NOW. Having Pilots trying to coordinate ourselves without having any bird's eye view or big picture is a recipe for accidents. It's so obvious and easy that we've got several different notes on the airport procedures. It's ridiculous and someone in safety needs to throw down the gauntlet with upper management or Airport Manager. That ramp is too congested and we've got too many daily aircraft movements back there to keep half-jobbing this thing. There's a reason that we don't just fire all the Ramp Controllers all over the country, because they keep aircraft moving and safe, BNA needs to realize this and act like it is a real airport, and stop acting like it is ZZZ airport or ZZZ1 airport. BNA needs a Ramp Controller, and they needed it a year ago, and will need it a year from now.
ASRSN:1951894.s: Pilots at BNA experienced a taxiway conflict while pushing back from Gate X due to the absence of a Ramp Controller. The tug stopped to avoid another aircraft, requiring a deep push to resolve the standoff, which the reporter attributes to unsafe self-coordination in a congested ramp environment.

ASRSN:1951917.n: About 30 to 35 minutes before departure ramp personnel turned on a large industrial portable lighting system that faced directly into the flight deck. The light was absolutely blinding to all of us. I called operations to have it turned off immediately as it had completely destroyed our night vision. He said he would 'try' to have the turned light off. Sorry that's an UNSAT answer. I then had to go down to the ramp about 10 minutes later to get someone to turn it off as there was no effort made to comply with the request to operations. Although the person I found was cooperative, he said they have no way to see the ramp which was puzzling because it was mainly on aircraft left. Regardless, I told him we have no night vision whatsoever and if they're not going to turn it off, I would delay departure until we can literally see again. I'm not exaggerating it was that bright directly facing us. You know there's a problem when it's XA PM and the pilots have to wear sunglasses.
ASRSN:1951917.s: Ramp personnel operated a portable light facing the flight deck 30 minutes before departure, blinding the pilots and destroying their night vision. The crew delayed departure until the light was turned off after operations failed to respond to their initial request.

ASRSN:1951924.n: I believe the 5G indicator for this flight was reflecting as indicator X/pass incorrectly. According to the Company NOTAM issued at the time, and the airport eligibility link in Dispatch Tool, ZZZ did not have any Airbus Alternate Means of Compliance approved. A detail to note - when I started my shift at XA:00 the indicator showed indicator Y, but at some point prior to release it turned to indicator X.
ASRSN:1951924.s: The pilot reported that the 5G indicator for a flight to ZZZ incorrectly displayed as X/pass, despite the airport lacking approved Airbus Alternate Means of Compliance. The indicator changed from Y to X between the pilot's shift start and flight release.

ASRSN:1951930.n: Aircraft X calls for taxi while tug was still underneath them. Instructions were given for taxi and immediately flight was told to hold position. Controller noticed the tug was still underneath. Once the tug appeared to be cleared, flight was given instructions to taxi. Pilot mentioned they were given all clear before they called for taxi.
ASRSN:1951930.s: Aircraft X requested taxi while a tug was still underneath, prompting the controller to issue a hold position after noticing the obstruction. The pilot reported receiving an all-clear prior to the request, but the aircraft was only cleared to taxi once the tug had moved.

ASRSN:1951935.n: On Date, assignment for my Move Team Department (Team 1) was to move Aircraft X from Terminal X to the Service Ramp Position XX. My assignment on Team X is Radio Observer (handle communication with ATCT). In communication with ATCT, instructions from Taxiway 1 held short of Runway XX Center, is to cross Runway XX Center, turn left Taxiway 2 contact Ground. Upon left turn onto Taxiway 1, Tow Tug began to slide, left on an angle (overcompensating) the left turn, and continued until stop, with the tow tug facing the number 1 engine of the aircraft, resulting in a Jack Knife Accident. Conditions during the incident, were after a brief snow flurry initially noticed at the beginning of transit prior to leaving Terminal X. The area where the incident took place had slight snow cover, while the Taxiway 1 is an incline prior to crossing the runway and then a DECLINE after crossing Runway. Fuel onboard Aircraft X was 35,600 pounds. Using Tug went to terminal and picked up Aircraft X off of Gate X also had a fuel weight of 35,600 pounds. Everything went as normal, now leading up to incident we are on Taxiway 1 and just crossed Runway XXC which Runways are pitched and need to give more gas to go over, and as we are turning onto Taxiway 2 I was doing about 10 MPH. I wanna say when I crossed the painted line that had ice and snow is when I lost control. There was no correcting as plane just started pushing us.
ASRSN:1951935.s: A Move Team Radio Observer reported a jackknife accident while towing Aircraft X from Terminal X to the Service Ramp on snowy, inclined Taxiway 1. The tow tug lost control and overcompensated during a left turn onto Taxiway 2 at 10 MPH, causing the tug to face the aircraft's number 1 engine due to ice and snow on the painted line.

ASRSN:1951947.n: Landing 25L near dusk, parking at FBO. There were two planes behind us, so we wanted to minimize our time on the runway. Stable approach. Touchdown in the TDZ. We both saw what appeared to be a taxiway, left turn off between G and A7. The Controller told us to turn right on H4. We complied. As we slowed and taxied to FBO per ATC's instructions, we realized that what we had seen was not a taxiway, but rather a piece of concrete that does not connect the runway to Taxiway A. It is not marked on any charts, though can be seen on web-based satellite images. If it had not been dusk, we might have been able to see the markings better, or the fact that it didn't connect. As it was dusk, it was the ATC instruction that prevented the excursion and shutting down LAX's arrivals.First, mark the pavement on taxi diagrams, so that we can brief the potential hazard. Second, mark the pavement better, maybe with something other than ground paint which is difficult to see at dusk.
ASRSN:1951947.s: Pilots landing on 25L at dusk mistook an unmarked concrete slab for a taxiway and intended to turn left, but ATC instructed a right turn onto H4. This clearance prevented a runway excursion caused by the uncharted pavement, which was difficult to distinguish from a taxiway in low light.

ASRSN:1951964.n: Runway 19 hold short line has been moved. Taxiway Juliet center line markings have been moved 75 feet west. There is a NOTAM for non-standard markings. This change has changed the Tower controller's options for aircraft movements at the hold short line. This is an accident waiting to happen! We were number 1 in the hold bay. Tower instructed us to pull up to the hold short line of Runway 19. Tower changed the plan and cleared a B737-800 to position and hold. This aircraft was holding short on the taxiway Juliet line. As the 737 started to roll it quickly became apparent that the left wingtip of 737 family aircraft hangs over the north-south hold short line by 15 to 20 feet. Same for A320 family aircraft. Luckily, the 737 pilot realized his left wing tip to my nose clearance was not sufficient and he moved off the taxiway Juliet line to allow enough clearance for him to taxi on the runway. Terrible engineering and measurements! Never should have moved the Juliet taxi line! Tower controllers had standard operating procedures and overnight they were made obsolete. Was any training conducted for Tower Controllers with new SOPs? Repaint the hold short lines back the way they were. If not, at least repaint the lines such that there is proper wing-tip clearance by making proper measurements!
ASRSN:1951964.s: A pilot reported that a B737-800 holding short of Runway 19 on a relocated Taxiway Juliet line had insufficient wingtip clearance due to non-standard markings. The 737 pilot aborted the movement to avoid a collision, highlighting a dangerous engineering change that rendered standard tower procedures obsolete.

ASRSN:1951978.n: Strong dirty sock smell fume event after entering flight deck plane taken out of service. Apparently was noticed by prior cabin crewKnown fume events have occurred on these aircraft. Illness and injuries have occurred to crew members Need a fix on the 321 fleet to prevent this from occurring. During preflight CA (Captain) and FO (First Officer) noticed an abnormal musty type of odor. Flight attendants were asked to verify if the odor was also present in the cabin. We were informed that they could not detect a smell but that they had noticed it during the inbound flight. Passengers were deplaned and Maintenance was notified.
ASRSN:1951978.s: The Captain and First Officer detected a strong musty odor on the flight deck of an A321 during preflight, which cabin crew confirmed was present on the inbound flight. Passengers were deplaned and the aircraft was taken out of service for maintenance due to the suspected fume event.

ASRSN:1952052.n: Aircraft X in ZZZ reported both Overwing exit door slides not showing armed. Technicians called Maintenance for approval to defer both of the O/W exit slide armed indications. Maintenance rejected the MELs pending an inspection of the OW exit slide arming lever engagement. Technicians went out and found on both doors the slide arming levers were not slid / engaged into the door frames. (if the doors were opened the slides would not have deployed). Aircraft X was 2 cycles post overhaul in ZZZ1 following storage. It had multiple test flights performed in ZZZ1, then did a repo flight to ZZZ2. At revenue flight to ZZZ was where this defect was discovered.
ASRSN:1952052.s: Technicians on Aircraft X discovered both overwing exit slide arming levers were disengaged during a revenue flight to ZZZ. Maintenance rejected deferring the defect, noting that slides would not have deployed if the doors were opened.

ASRSN:1952055.n: Good morning, we had an incident here at Gate XX at approximately XA40. Operations called us to go to Gate XX to investigate Aircraft X, Engine 2 regarding a fuel leak. I went out with Person A, the midnight Lead and we were ready to investigate the leak while the crew ran the engine since it was a full flight and ready to go. Once we got there the crew told the ramp that operation had given them the green light to push out to the alley even though we in maintenance objected. We did not think going out to the alley while the Ramp was pushing the aircraft would be the best choice since the aircraft was still at the Gate. We were overridden by Operations and the Crew asked the Ramp to push back to the alley. I followed the aircraft to the alley while the ramp positioned the aircraft on the center line. As the crew started #2 engine and began to run I noticed fuel was not dripping out but gushing out the bottom and spraying the aft end of the engine. I was yelling at the crew to stop the engine and it took about 10 seconds or so for anyone to acknowledge what I was asking. At this point I was not sure what type of leak we had and instructed the Ramp to bring the aircraft back to the Gate. They began to bring the aircraft back to the Gate. I went back in to gather more guys to help out. By the time we went back out the aircraft was back on the center line and the engine was running again. The ramp said that operations stopped the aircraft from coming back to the Gate and they were instructed to push back out and have the crew run the engine and observe for leaks. Supposedly the leak stopped and the aircraft left. I personally witnessed the engine spraying fuel from the bottom and the ramp did not. They should NOT be observing for leaks since they did not even see an active stream and this procedure is dangerous. We had people on board with an engine spraying fuel out as it started which can lead to a fire. I was beyond livid from what I experienced this morning. Most of us take pride in our work and regard safety of the passengers as our PRIMARY concern. What I witnessed this morning was everything but that. I called Maintenance Control to voice my concern because originally we were told that they made the decision. After speaking to one of them they said it came from OUR operations here. We have new hires and this is not the way they should be observing our maintenance program to be run. We should not be sending aircraft to the centerline to run an engine when it has been reported by the ramp and/or crew that there is a leak and have the ramp determine if there is a leak.
ASRSN:1952055.s: Maintenance and crew investigated a reported fuel leak on Aircraft X at Gate XX, but Operations overrode maintenance objections to push the aircraft to the alley for an engine run. The reporter witnessed Engine 2 gushing fuel, creating a fire risk with passengers on board, yet Operations ordered the aircraft to depart after the leak reportedly stopped.

ASRSN:1952058.n: Positioned the loader, opened door, putting up the bridge, bent the panel. They called maintenance. Maintenance went up, remove the panel off and the plane went out with a delay. Notified my Crew Chief, Management, and they called Maintenance.
ASRSN:1952058.s: Ground crew bent a panel while positioning a loader and erecting a bridge. Maintenance removed the damaged panel, causing a departure delay after the Crew Chief and management were notified.

ASRSN:1952061.n: I was flying in a complex plane for the first time after earning my complex endorsement. I did a complete pre-flight and didn't notice anything amiss. However, when I did the idle check during run-up, it did act a little unusual. I attributed it at the time to the cold weather, but in hindsight, it was probably related to the problem I experienced. Specifically, when I pulled the throttle for the idle check, the power did not drop smoothly - audibly, it cut smoothly to maybe 25% and then sputtered a bit, then it dropped all the way down to idle. It did smooth out at idle though. I was still able to successfully increase power back to 1,000 RPM, and while taxing to the runway, I successfully increased and decreased throttle with no issue. I departed southeast from ZZZ, headed around south of the city to reach a lake, with the goal of flying into ZZZ1 along the river. I configured the engine to 25 squared successfully enroute. After getting to the lake, which is the southern end of a noise abatement corridor into ZZZ1, I turned north and decreased throttle to descend below the Bravo shelf. However, I began to pick up speed. I noticed that the engine was now running at 24 inches with 2,500 RPM. I pulled the throttle back to what should have been idle, but engine power did not change. At this point, I turned east to avoid running into ZZZ1 or ZZZ2 airspace while I diagnosed the problem. I pushed the prop back up to full forward so as to play with the throttle a bit. I was able to push the throttle up to max successfully, but I could not bring it below 23-24 inches. Each time I went to max throttle and back down again, it felt like it settled at slightly different pressures between 22 and 24 inches, but I am not sure if I imagined that. I tried cycling the throttle up and down a few times, but the bottom remained stubbornly high. At this point, I turned westbound to head back to ZZZ. At the lowest settings I could manage, the lowest speed I could get to in cruise, I was maintaining about 133 KIAS. So as to get below max gear extension speed (130 KIAS), I entered a brief climb, and dropped the gear when I hit 130. Gear down and a slight climb then brought the speed just low enough to barely get into the white arc, so I progressively put in full flaps. With gear down, zero throttle, and full flaps, I was maintaining altitude at around 90 KIAS, which is 20 KIAS over best approach speed on descent, so I knew this was going to be a fast and floaty landing at best. At this point, I was 15 NM southeast of ZZZ, so I called and [requested priority handling] from ZZZ Tower. They cleared me to land XXL, so I did a very long shallow approach so as to avoid picking up speed. About 50 ft. from the threshold, I was at 95 KIAS, at which point I pulled the mixture and did a power-off glide to the runway, floated a long way but landed successfully, and then rolled onto a taxiway before stopping.To be honest, I only feel like I was able to deal with this situation because of my training on the fundamentals of flight. We never practiced anything like it, but I knew I had to slow that plane down by any means necessary, and that picking up speed on approach could be fatal. I am honestly still a bit worried as to what I would have need to have done if the throttle had been stuck full instead of 75%. I suppose I would have tried putting the gear down during a much more aggressive climb. But a faster landing would have been even more harrowing. My adrenaline was through the roof after landing - it took several hours to come down off of it.
ASRSN:1952061.s: A pilot flying a complex aircraft experienced a throttle malfunction en route that prevented reducing manifold pressure below 23-24 inches. The pilot managed a high-speed approach and landing at ZZZ by using gear, flaps, and mixture cutoff to control speed, attributing the safe outcome to fundamental flight training.
